As an example of the CLT in practice, see Fig.\ \@ref(fig:CLTDemoLatex), where samples of various sizes are taken from $\text{Gamma}(2, 1)$ distributions.
The sampling distribution of the sample mean appears more like an approximate normal as the sample size gets larger, and the approximation is reasoably good even for $n = 10$.



```{r, CLTDemoLatex, fig.align="center", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Exact sampling distribution of the mean (solid lines) overlaid with the CLT normal approximation (dashed lines). The samples are drawn from a Gamma$(2, 1)$ distribution.", out.width='100%', fig.width=7}
# Gamma(alpha=2, rate=1): Xbar ~ Gamma(n*alpha, rate=n)
# mu = 2, sigma = sqrt(2)

alpha <- 2
beta  <- 1
mu    <- alpha / beta
sg    <- sqrt(alpha) / beta

ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 25, 50, 100)

# Build x grid and densities for each n
traces <- lapply(ns, function(n) {
  se   <- sg / sqrt(n)
  x    <- seq(max(mu - 5*se, 1e-4), 
              mu + 5*se, 
              length.out = 600)
  yex  <- dgamma(x, 
                 shape = n * alpha, 
                 rate = n * beta)
  yclt <- dnorm(x,  
                mean  = mu,        
                sd   = se)
  list(x = x, 
       yex = yex, 
       yclt = yclt, 
       n = n)
})

# Build figure
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

plot(x = traces[[1]]$x, 
     y = traces[[1]]$yex,
     type = "l",
     xlab = expression(bar(italic(X))),
     ylab = "",
     axes = FALSE,
     main = expression(Sample~size*":"~italic(n)==1),
     lwd = 2)
axis(side = 1)
lines(x = traces[[1]]$x, 
      y = traces[[1]]$yclt,
      lty = 2,
      lwd = 2)





plot(x = traces[[2]]$x,
